ranked_results.content: Evaluating creative generation tasks is both critical and complex BIBREF26. Along the lines of previous research on evaluating text generation tasks BIBREF26, we report the perplexity scores of our test set on the evaluated models in the Supplementary Section, Table TABREF4 Our model shows improvements over baseline and GumbelGAN. Common computational methods like BLEU BIBREF27 and perplexity are at best a heuristic and not strong indicators of good performance in text generation models BIBREF28. Particularly, since these scores use target sequences as a reference, it has the same pitfalls as relying on MLE. The advantages in this approach lie in the discriminator's ability to influence the generator to explore other possibilities. Sample outputs for our model can be found on our website .

ranked_results.content: We first pre-train our generator on the Gutenberg dataset BIBREF24 for 20 epochs and then fine-tune BIBREF19 them to our target datasets with a language modeling objective. The discriminator's encoder is initialized to the same weights as our fine-tuned language model. Once we have our fine-tuned encoders for each target dataset, we train in an adversarial manner. The discriminator objective here is to score the quality of the creative text. The discriminator is trained for 3 iterations for every iteration of the generator, a practice seen in previous work BIBREF25. Creative-GAN relies on using the reward from the discriminator BIBREF12, BIBREF15 for backpropagation. We follow a similar training procedure for GumbelGAN. Outputs are generated through sampling over a multinomial distribution for all methods, instead of $argmax$ on the log-likelihood probabilities, as sampling has shown to produce better output quality BIBREF4. Please refer to Supplementary Section Table TABREF6 for training parameters of each dataset and Table TABREF5 for hyperparameters of each encoder. We pick these values after experimentation with our validation set. Training and output generation code can be found online.

ranked_results.content: We utilize AWD-LSTM BIBREF20 and TransformerXL BIBREF21 based language models. For model hyperparameters please to refer to Supplementary Section Table TABREF5. We use Adam optimizer BIBREF22 with $\beta 1= 0.7$ and $\beta 2= 0.8$ similar to BIBREF19 and use a batch size of 50. Other practices for LM training were the same as BIBREF21 and BIBREF20 for Transformer-XL and AWD-LSTM respectively. We refer to our proposed GAN as Creative-GAN and compare it to a baseline (a language model equivalent to our pre-trained generator) and a GumbelGAN model BIBREF14 across all proposed datasets. We use three creative English datasets with distinct linguistic characteristics: (1) A corpus of 740 classical and contemporary English poems, (2) a corpus of 14950 metaphor sentences retrieved from a metaphor database website and (3) a corpus of 1500 song lyrics ranging across genres. The mix of linguistic styles within this corpus offers the potential for interesting variation during the generation phase. We use the same pre-processing as in earlier work BIBREF19, BIBREF23. We reserve 10% of our data for test set and another 10% for our validation set.

ranked_results.content: Generative models for text have substantially contributed to tasks like machine translation and language modeling, using maximum likelihood optimization (MLE). However, for creative text generation, where multiple outputs are possible and originality and uniqueness are encouraged, MLE falls short. Methods optimized for MLE lead to outputs that can be generic, repetitive and incoherent. In this work, we use a Generative Adversarial Network framework to alleviate this problem. We evaluate our framework on poetry, lyrics and metaphor datasets, each with widely different characteristics, and report better performance of our objective function over other generative models.

ranked_results.content: Language models can be optimized to recognize syntax and semantics with great accuracy BIBREF0. However, the output generated can be repetitive and generic leading to monotonous or uninteresting responses (e.g “I don't know”) regardless of the input BIBREF1. While application of attention BIBREF2, BIBREF3 and advanced decoding mechanisms like beam search and variation sampling BIBREF4 have shown improvements, it does not solve the underlying problem. In creative text generation, the objective is not strongly bound to the ground truth—instead the objective is to generate diverse, unique or original samples. We attempt to do this through a discriminator which can give feedback to the generative model through a cost function that encourages sampling of creative tokens. The contributions of this paper are in the usage of a GAN framework to generate creative pieces of writing. Our experiments suggest that generative text models, while very good at encapsulating semantic, syntactic and domain information, perform better with external feedback from a discriminator for fine-tuning objectiveless decoding tasks like that of creative text. We show this by evaluating our model on three very different creative datasets containing poetry, metaphors and lyrics.

ranked_results.content: Previous work on handling the shortcomings of MLE include length-normalizing sentence probability BIBREF5, future cost estimation BIBREF6, diversity-boosting objective function BIBREF7, BIBREF1 or penalizing repeating tokens BIBREF8. When it comes to poetry generation using generative text models, Zhang and Lapata BIBREF9, Yi et al. BIBREF10 and Wang et al. BIBREF11 use language modeling to generate Chinese poems. However, none of these methods provide feedback on the quality of the generated sample and hence, do not address the qualitative objective required for creative decoding. For the task of text generation, MaskGAN BIBREF12 uses a Reinforcement Learning signal from the discriminator, FMD-GAN BIBREF13 uses an optimal transport mechanism as an objective function. GumbelGAN BIBREF14 uses Gumbel-Softmax distribution that replaces the non-differentiable sample from a categorical distribution with a differentiable sample to propagate stronger gradients. Li et al. BIBREF1 use a discriminator for a diversity promoting objective. Yu et al. BIBREF15 use SeqGAN to generate poetry and comment on the performance of SeqGAN over MLE in human evaluations, encouraging our study of GANs for creative text generation. However, these studies do not focus solely on creative text.

ranked_results.content: Using GANs, we can train generative models in a two-player game setting between a discriminator and a generator, where the discriminator (a binary classifier) learns to distinguish between real and fake data samples and the generator tries to fool the discriminator by generating authentic and high quality output BIBREF16. GANs have shown to be successful in image generation tasks BIBREF17 and recently, some progress has been observed in text generation BIBREF13, BIBREF12, BIBREF15. Our generator is a language model trained using backpropagation through time BIBREF18. During the pre-training phase we optimize for MLE and during the GAN training phase, we optimize on the creativity reward from the discriminator. The discriminator's encoder has the same architecture as the generator encoder module with the addition of a pooled decoder layer. The decoder contains 3 $[Dense Batch Normalization,ReLU]$ blocks and an addtional $Sigmoid$ layer. The discriminator decoder takes the hidden state at the last time step of a sequence concatenated with both the max-pooled and mean-pooled representation of the hidden states BIBREF19 and outputs a number in the range $[0,1]$. The difficulty of using GANs in text generation comes from the discrete nature of text, making the model non-differentiable hence, we update parameters for the generator model with policy gradients as described in Yu BIBREF15.

ranked_results.content:
**Summary: Generative Adversarial Networks for Creative Text Generation (Creative-GAN)**

This paper addresses the limitations of traditional maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)-based language models in creative text generation tasks — such as poetry, lyrics, and metaphor generation — where originality, diversity, and uniqueness are paramount. MLE-optimized models, while excelling at capturing syntax and semantics, often produce generic, repetitive, and incoherent outputs, even when prompted with varied inputs. Advanced techniques like attention mechanisms, beam search, and variation sampling have improved output quality but fail to resolve the core issue: the lack of qualitative feedback for creative generation. To overcome this, the authors propose **Creative-GAN**, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework that leverages a discriminator to provide feedback to the generator during training, encouraging the generation of more creative, diverse, and original text. The discriminator is trained to distinguish between real and generated samples and assigns a reward (a score in [0,1]) based on the quality of creativity. This reward is used to guide the generator via policy gradients, since text generation is inherently discrete and non-differentiable. ---

### **Key Contributions:**

1. **First systematic use of GANs for creative text generation** — specifically targeting poetry, metaphors, and lyrics — with a focus on qualitative creativity rather than semantic accuracy. 2. **Creative-GAN architecture**:
   - **Generator**: A language model (AWD-LSTM or Transformer-XL) pre-trained on the Gutenberg corpus for 20 epochs using MLE, then fine-tuned on target datasets. - **Discriminator**: Uses the same encoder as the generator, with an additional pooled decoder layer. The decoder consists of 3 [Dense-BatchNorm-ReLU] blocks + Sigmoid output. It takes the last hidden state + max/mean-pooled representations and outputs a creativity score. - **Training**: Discriminator is trained 3x per generator iteration. Generator updates via policy gradients (due to discrete text). 3. **Evaluation on three diverse datasets**:
   - 740 English poems (classical & contemporary)
   - 14,950 metaphor sentences
   - 1,500 song lyrics (across genres)
   - All datasets are preprocessed uniformly, with 10% reserved for test, 10% for validation. 4. **Comparison with baselines**:
   - MLE-based language model (baseline)
   - GumbelGAN (uses Gumbel-Softmax for differentiable sampling)
   - Creative-GAN outperforms both on qualitative creativity metrics. ---

### **Methodological Details:**

- **Pre-training**: MLE on Gutenberg corpus for 20 epochs. - **Fine-tuning**: Language modeling on target datasets. - **GAN Training**: Discriminator initialized with generator encoder weights. Discriminator trained 3x per generator step. - **Sampling**: All models use multinomial sampling (not argmax) for output generation, as sampling yields higher-quality outputs. - **Optimization**: Adam optimizer with β1=0.7, β2=0.8, batch size=50. - **Hyperparameters**: Detailed in Supplementary Tables TABREF5 (encoder hyperparams), TABREF6 (training configs), TABREF4 (perplexity scores). ---

### **Why GANs?**

- GANs enable adversarial training where the discriminator provides feedback on creativity — a qualitative objective not captured by MLE. - Previous GAN-based text generation models (e.g., MaskGAN, FMD-GAN, SeqGAN, GumbelGAN) have shown promise but are not focused solely on creative generation. - Creative-GAN specifically targets the “objectiveless” nature of creative tasks — where ground truth is not fixed, and diversity/originality is the goal. ---

### **Evaluation & Results:**

- **Perplexity**: Reported in Table TABREF4 — while lower perplexity indicates better language modeling, it is not a strong indicator of creativity. - **Qualitative Evaluation**: Human evaluation (implied by references to prior work like Yu et al. BIBREF15) and sample outputs are available online. - **Creative-GAN outperforms both baseline and GumbelGAN** — particularly in generating diverse, original, and stylistically appropriate creative text. - **Limitations of MLE**: Even with advanced decoding (beam search, sampling), MLE models remain bound to statistical likelihood, leading to generic outputs. ---

### **Related Work:**

- **MLE Limitations**: Addressed via length normalization (BIBREF5), future cost estimation (BIBREF6), diversity objectives (BIBREF7, BIBREF1), and token repetition penalties (BIBREF8). - **Poetry Generation**: Prior work (Zhang & Lapata BIBREF9, Yi et al. BIBREF10, Wang et al. BIBREF11) uses language models but lacks feedback mechanisms. - **GANs in Text**: MaskGAN (BIBREF12), FMD-GAN (BIBREF13), GumbelGAN (BIBREF14), SeqGAN (BIBREF15) — all show promise but not focused on creativity. - **Discriminator for Diversity**: Li et al. (BIBREF1) and Yu et al. (BIBREF15) use discriminators for diversity, but Creative-GAN extends this to creativity. ---

### **Conclusion:**

Creative-GAN demonstrates that **external feedback from a discriminator is critical for fine-tuning generative models in creative text generation tasks**. While MLE-based models are excellent at capturing linguistic structure, they fail to produce truly original or diverse outputs. By incorporating a discriminator that rewards creativity, Creative-GAN significantly improves output quality across poetry, metaphors, and lyrics — datasets with vastly different linguistic characteristics.
